meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'ождать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'wait', paired with 'ждать'.

examples.trans: Wait, I'll be right there.
Wait a minute.

examples.text: Подожди, Нин, ты не поняла. Это же стыдно!
examples.trans: Wait, Nina, you don't get it. It's shameful!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Please get acquainted.
Denis, this is my mom.
Mom, this is my boyfriend Denis.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'where', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Никто не видел, где все тележки?
examples.trans: Has anyone seen where all the carts are?
And where is our fur seal?

examples.text: Где норка? Я же договорилась с директором зоопарка.
examples.trans: Where is the mink? I made an arrangement with the zoo director.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'our, ours', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Это хозяйка нашего отеля, Элеонора Андреевна.
examples.trans: This is the owner of our hotel, Eleonora Andreevna.
Our head cook there got sick.

examples.text: Нам нужно решить нашу деликатную проблему.
examples.trans: We need to solve our delicate problem.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'snake' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Нагиев совсем не изменился за это время!
examples.trans: Nagiyev has not changed at all during this time!
Many people consider snakes very cute.

examples.text: Но на змею придётся сегодня скинуться.
examples.trans: But we will have to chip in for the snake today.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'only', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: They just fired me.

examples.text: По контракту только я могу увольнять.
examples.trans: Under the contract, only I can fire cooks.

examples.text: Дима, я тебя только очень прошу.
examples.trans: Dima, I only ask you very much.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you (polite/plural)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Denis, and what do you do for a living?
You are under my roof now.

examples.text: Мне нужно срочно выйти на воздух!
examples.trans: I need to step outside for fresh air urgently!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'but, after all', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Yes, I already know that.

examples.text: Очень хорошо, и к Кате поближе.
examples.trans: Very good, and closer to Katya.

examples.text: Тебя вспомнишь — и уже не так плохо.
examples.trans: One remembers you, and things do not seem so bad.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'ourselves', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Do not be afraid, you will manage on your own.
Blow into this tube yourself.
To that same cursed room.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'she; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Она ничего об этом не знала.
examples.trans: She knew nothing about it.

examples.text: Она выгонит нас, чтобы вас унизить.
examples.trans: She will kick us out to humiliate you.

examples.text: За что она хотела меня уволить?
examples.trans: Why did she want to fire me?

meanings.en: to cook, to make (food), to prepare
meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'готовить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'cooked, prepared', paired with 'готовить'.

examples.text: Чтобы вкусно её для вас приготовить.
examples.trans: In order to cook it deliciously for you.

examples.text: Только вы же сами её приготовили!
examples.trans: But you cooked it yourself!
I cooked an ordinary eel today.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Yes, I already know that.
I always remembered her.
Actually, he died recently.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'really, can it be', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And I warmed it up for you.
Let her undress him herself.

examples.text: Да разве я похож на злодея?
examples.trans: Do I really look like a villain?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Denis, this is my mom.
Very nice to meet you.
Do not be afraid, Mom does not bite.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'хожий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('look like, similar').

examples.text: Да разве я похож на злодея?
examples.trans: Do I really look like a villain?
You look like janitors.
He looks very much like his father.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Please get acquainted.
Yes, I already know that.
I work as a cook in the kitchen.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'villain, scoundrel' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Да разве я похож на злодея?

examples.text: Ну злодеи они там все, конечно!
examples.trans: Well, they are all villains in there, of course!
At the end of the film they caught the villain.

meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'ычный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('ordinary, usual').

examples.trans: I cooked an ordinary eel today.

examples.text: Да нет на него никакого компромата. Обычный мужик.
examples.trans: There is no compromising material on him at all. Just an ordinary guy.
It was an ordinary day.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'горь'). Common masculine noun meaning 'eel' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Look for another head chef for yourselves.

examples.text: Катя сегодня уезжает в другой город.
examples.trans: Katya is leaving for another city today.

examples.text: За сто тысяч я спасу кого угодно!
examples.trans: For a hundred thousand I will save anyone!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'егодня').

examples.text: Катя сегодня уезжает в другой город.
examples.trans: Katya is leaving for another city today.
Thank goodness, we dodged a bullet today!

examples.text: Давай сегодня спокойно, я тебя умоляю.
examples.trans: Let's keep it calm today, I beg you.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('living').

examples.trans: These are rare animals for the evening.

examples.text: Все деньги пойдут на спасение животных.
examples.trans: All the money will go toward saving the animals.

examples.text: Мне на вечере нужны милые животные.
examples.trans: I need cute animals at the evening.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Denis, and what do you do for a living?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'into the pot' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: А живую змею в кастрюлю спрятал.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'прятать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'hid', paired with 'прятать'.

examples.text: А живую змею в кастрюлю спрятал.
examples.trans: And I hid the live snake in a pot.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'крыть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'opened', paired with 'открывать'.

examples.trans: It pushed the lid open and crawled away!
Open the door.
Open the window.

examples.trans: It pushed the lid open and crawled away!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'now', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You are under my roof now.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Денис, быстро иди работать на кухню!
examples.trans: Denis, quickly go work in the kitchen!
Now quickly look for it everywhere!
Yes, come on faster, let's start!

meanings.note: Prefix 'ис-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (stem 'кать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'look for / search'.

examples.trans: I'm looking for a job.
What are you looking for?

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
examples.trans: Well, happy now? Now I have to look for a new job.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'everywhere', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Now quickly look for it everywhere!
There's water everywhere!

examples.text: А я недавно большой кредит взял.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'to', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'table, desk' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: So we will see each other often.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'лзать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'crawl'.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Go on, crawl around and search carefully!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'let's', paired with 'дать'.

examples.text: Давай сегодня спокойно, я тебя умоляю.
examples.trans: Let's keep it calm today, I beg you.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'lady, woman' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Старый кредит отдам и новый возьму.
examples.trans: I will pay off the old loan and take a new one.

examples.text: Давайте, дамы и господа, наполним бокалы!
examples.trans: Come on, ladies and gentlemen, let's fill our glasses!

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'gentlemen' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Давайте, дамы и господа, наполним бокалы!
examples.trans: Come on, ladies and gentlemen, let's fill our glasses!
Gentlemen, I apologise.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'полнить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'we will fill'.

related.gloss: not to we will fill (negated infinitive)

examples.text: Давайте, дамы и господа, наполним бокалы!
examples.trans: Come on, ladies and gentlemen, let's fill our glasses!

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и наполнить вовремя.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'glasses' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Come on, ladies and gentlemen, let's fill our glasses!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'all', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I still have to inspect the whole hotel.
Everything's fine.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'together', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Let's all have a drink together right now.

examples.text: Я так рада, что мы работаем вместе!
examples.trans: I am so glad that we work together!
We're together.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.trans: Vitya, meet her right now.

examples.text: Сейчас попрощаемся, выпьем, и всё будет хорошо.
examples.trans: Right now we will say goodbye, have a drink, and all will be fine.
And where are you going right now?

meanings.en: to drink up, to have a drink
meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'пить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'we will have a drink', paired with 'выпивать'.

examples.trans: Oh, I've had a bit to drink now.
Drink some water.
May I drink a tiny drop of beer?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'where to', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Then do not be in a hurry.

I am not leaving here for anywhere.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'could', paired with 'смочь'.

examples.trans: Denis, can you help me, please?
I can't today.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'this', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Denis, this is my mom.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'деяться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'hope', paired with 'понадеяться'.

examples.trans: I hope you understood me.
I hope so. Go on, act quickly!
I hope so.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Very nice to meet you.

I work as a cook in the kitchen.

examples.trans: We need to do everything and bites on time.
